name: st_shape_change
description: How the ST segment's shape changed at the candidate's extremum, measured against the same lead's own beats rather than as an absolute contour. Per involved lead (peak lead first), from the 15-s averaged beats: J point, ST point (J+80 ms below 100 bpm, earlier at higher heart rate, the LTSTDB convention, K21), J-to-ST slope, T-wave extreme and QRS amplitude at the extremum, and the same values in two references: 'before' (10 min to 30 s before onset, outside all candidates) and 'matched_hr' (windows outside all candidates within 5 bpm of the extremum's heart rate, within 2 h). For each reference: the change at the J point, at the ST point and of the T wave, signed towards the candidate (positive = in the candidate's direction), share_of_st_point_change_present_at_j (about 1 = parallel shift, above 1.5 = change concentrated at J, below 0.67 = change concentrated at the ST point; engineering defaults) and a one-line pattern. It turns the Long-Term ST Database shape terms quoted in the reference knowledge into numbers relative to the patient's own beat, so a lead whose ST segment is upsloping at all times is not mistaken for a new upsloping change. How to read it, in both directions, using the 'before' reference first: (1) Depression concentrated at the J point, with the ST point changing much less (the segment more upsloping than before), is the 'J point depression with positive slope' of the heart-rate related class and argues against ischemia; if the ST-point change itself is still about 200 uV or more, K24 and K25 disagree and it counts neither way. (2) Depression concentrated at the ST point (the segment less upsloping or more downsloping than before) is the 'horizontal flattening; down sloping' of the ischemic class and argues for ischemia, the more so the larger the ST-point change (K26). (3) A parallel shift does not by itself separate the classes (the heart-rate related class lists 'parallel shift of ST segment'): judge it by the absolute slope at the extremum and the depth (Context, heart-rate reading 3). (4) Elevation with the J point raised about as much as the ST point is a true ST elevation (the ischemic class lists 'elevation'; Context, ST-elevation guidance) and argues for ischemia when the change is gradual and without a QRS step. (5) Elevation concentrated at the ST point with a T-wave change of at least twice the ST-point change is the T wave rising into the measuring point ('moving of T-wave into ST segment; T-wave peaking', heart-rate related class) rather than a raised segment, and argues against ischemia. (6) 'little change against this reference' means the deviation was already present before onset (a fragment or the lead's usual level; read episode_context). The matched_hr reference asks the same question with heart rate held about equal: a large J or ST-point change there means heart rate alone does not explain the change; little change there means the patient's ST at this heart rate usually looks like this (weigh with rate_response; it fits a heart-rate related change but does not exclude demand ischemia). Limits: 'before' may be at a different heart rate, and when st_point_ms_after_j differs between reference and extremum part of the ST-point change comes from measuring at another point of a sloping segment; a reference with few windows, or a noisy lead, is weak. A QRS amplitude ratio far from 1 fits the axis-shift description quoted in the reference knowledge, but ischemia can also change QRS amplitude gradually (K18, K19): check morphology_steps for a step before reading it as position. Supplied in the initial dossier. A measurement packet, not a diagnosis.
